title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what moves, what refuses to move, and who is speaking

questions.prompt: At the end of a visit to a workshop in Sousse, two pupils questioned the engineer. Hedi asked her: "Where do you test the prototypes?" Rania asked her: "Do you work with a team?" The next morning the engineer tells a colleague what the two of them wanted to know. Which line reports both questions correctly?

options.text: Hedi asked me where did I test the prototypes, and Rania asked me did I work with a team.
Hedi asked me where I tested the prototypes, and Rania asked me that I worked with a team.
Hedi asked me where I tested the prototypes, and Rania asked me if I worked with a team.
Hedi asked me where was I testing the prototypes, and Rania asked me whether did I work with a team.

questions.explanation: Hedi asked me where I tested the prototypes, and Rania asked me if I worked with a team is right, and it is right twice over. A reported question stops being a question: it takes the word order of a statement and drops the do, does or did of the original, so where do you test becomes where I tested. A wh- question keeps its own question word, where; a yes/no question has no question word of its own and must borrow if, or whether, which is just as correct. And since the engineer reports the next morning, asked is a past, so test and work both step back to tested and worked, while you, who was the engineer, becomes I. Hedi asked me where did I test the prototypes, and Rania asked me did I work with a team keeps the interrogative machinery in both halves, as if the inverted commas were still there. Hedi asked me where I tested the prototypes, and Rania asked me that I worked with a team gets the first half right and then replaces if with that, which turns Rania's question into a statement she never made. And Hedi asked me where was I testing the prototypes, and Rania asked me whether did I work with a team inverts the subject in the first half and keeps did after whether in the second: whether and if are followed by a statement, never by a question.

questions.prompt: On Monday, four members of the club each said one sentence. On Friday the secretary writes them all up, and each time she begins with the same three words, She said that. In which of the four sentences does the verb stay exactly as it is?

options.text: I might come back for the second session.
I am writing the report at home this evening.
I have finished the poster.
I will bring the long cable from the storeroom.

questions.explanation: I might come back for the second session is the one: might belongs to the small group of modals that have nowhere to step back to, with would, should, ought to, had better, used to, could and must, and it is written the same in the report as in the words themselves, She said that she might come back. The other three all move, and each one shows a different line of the table. I am writing the report at home this evening is a present continuous, and after a past reporting verb it becomes a past continuous, she was writing. I have finished the poster is a present perfect, which steps back one notch. And I will bring the long cable from the storeroom is a future, and a future reported from the past becomes would bring; will is exactly the modal that does move, which is why learning the short list of those that do not is worth as much as learning the table.

questions.prompt: Last week, in front of the whole club, Rania said: "I have lost my password twice since September." Today it is Rania herself who is writing the club's report, and she has to put that sentence of her own into it. Which line does the job?

options.text: She said that I had lost my password twice since September.
I said that I had lost my password twice since September.
Rania said that I had lost her password twice since September.
I said that she had lost her password twice since September.

questions.explanation: I said that I had lost my password twice since September is right. The pronouns and the possessives of a report move to the third person because the person speaking is no longer the person writing, and here those two people are the same woman: Rania is reporting her own words, so I and my stay exactly where they were. The tense moves in the ordinary way, since said is a past. I said that she had lost her password twice since September is the trap the rule is made for: it applies the third person mechanically and hands Rania's password to somebody else. She said that I had lost my password twice since September turns the writer into a third person while keeping the first person inside the report, so the reader is told that some other woman lost the writer's password. And Rania said that I had lost her password twice since September commits both faults at once, naming Rania outside the report and leaving I inside it.

questions.prompt: The grammar table of lesson 26 gives a second way of building the same gradual change: the comparative of the adjective, then and, then the same comparative again. The table prints that line without a single example beside it. Which of these four sentences builds it correctly?

options.text: The queue at the library desk is getting more and more long.
The queue at the library desk is getting longer and long.
The queue at the library desk is getting long and longer.
The queue at the library desk is getting longer and longer.

questions.explanation: The queue at the library desk is getting longer and longer is right on both counts: long has one syllable, so its comparative is longer and not more long, and the structure repeats that comparative whole on each side of and. The queue at the library desk is getting more and more long builds the comparative with more, which English reserves for the longer adjectives, more and more crowded, more and more expensive; with a short adjective it is the ending -er that carries the comparison. The queue at the library desk is getting longer and long and The queue at the library desk is getting long and longer each leave one half in the plain form, and half a structure carries none of its meaning: both sides of and have to be comparatives, which is the whole idea of two comparatives joined by and.

questions.prompt: Four sentences from a science page, each using one word of the lesson. In one of them the word is used in a way its meaning does not allow, and the sentence contradicts itself. Which one?

options.text: The engineer assumes that the two machines will behave in the same way.
Two of the three prototypes survived the whole of the heat test.
A substantial number of pupils, three out of two hundred, returned the form.
The reason for the fall in the price of memory is obvious in the second column of the table.

questions.explanation: A substantial number of pupils, three out of two hundred, returned the form is the sentence that breaks: substantial means large in size or in amount, and the very figures the sentence gives, three out of two hundred, are as small as a number can well be. The writer meant a tiny number, or a handful. The other three use their word exactly as the lesson does. The engineer assumes that the two machines will behave in the same way takes something as true without having proved it, which is what assume is for. Two of the three prototypes survived the whole of the heat test says they came through a hard test without being destroyed. And The reason for the fall in the price of memory is obvious in the second column of the table says the reason can be seen there without anybody explaining it.

questions.prompt: The phrasal verb break up carries several everyday senses, and only the words standing round it say which one is meant. In which of these four sentences does it mean that a relationship between two people has come to an end?

options.text: The meeting broke up at six and everybody went home.
The two of them broke up after a year of arguing.
The signal broke up in the tunnel and we lost the call.
He broke up the old crate and used the wood for the fire.

questions.explanation: The two of them broke up after a year of arguing carries the sense the lesson uses: two people whose relationship comes to an end. Everything that decides it is in the words round the verb, the two of them and a year of arguing. The meeting broke up at six and everybody went home uses the sense a gathering takes: it came to an end and the people in it dispersed, which is why everybody went home follows so naturally. The signal broke up in the tunnel and we lost the call describes a sound or a picture that becomes broken and unclear, the sense you meet on a telephone. And He broke up the old crate and used the wood for the fire is the most concrete sense of all, an object smashed into pieces, and here the pieces are named in the second half of the sentence. One verb, four senses, and no way to choose between them except by reading what stands beside it.
